messages.body_plain:
Hi Holly,

Depending on the size of the data set (e.g., number of sites), it might be the case that the global model is simply over parameterized. If you think about it in terms of ‘unique’ covariate combinations, if you have as many as you do sites for example, this could result in ‘singularity’. If you could a little more info about the data that might help diagnose the problem.

You could also check those covariates for collinearity (correlations among the predictors) and remove covariates based on high correlations – usually you would keep the ones that are of more interest to you.

Regarding sub-models, I don’t have a suggestion for that, but if you are able to remove correlated covariates that might get you a ‘subset’.

Chris

messages.subject_clean: zero-inflated / highly skewed PREDICTORS
messages.body_plain:
Morning all,

I have been fitting some occupancy (and other) models recently using covariates that are highly skewed / zero-inflated. This question is not really realted to unmarked the package, but I feel like the answer, which I am sure some of you will have, will be inforamtive for unamrked analyses (but apologies if i am wrong!).

I am trying to find some guidance on how to treat highly skewed / zero-inflated PREDICTORS in a model, say a landcover type where ~80 % of the data are 0’s and 20% >0. In my head it seems clear to me that the zeros add an enormous amount of noise that detract from estimating a relationship of interest that exists in the non-zero parameter space. My current thinking about this issue would be to model the zeros explicitly:

y_{i} = b_{0} + b_{1} * I(cov=0) + b_{2} * cov + e_{i}

i.e., an intercept for the zeros and a coefficient for the relationship in the non-zero space. I did a small simulation study to see if a simple regression model can recover parameters from data generated under this model and it all checks out, but is it the recommended thing to do? Imagine also if all 5 or 20 or whatever covariates were like this?

Okay, so in short, I know that there are typically no assumptions about the distribution of the predictors in regression type analyses, so I am wondering, although the predictor has no assumed distribution, does a large amount of zero inflation influence the ability to detect an effect of the non-zero stuff.

If anyone knows of some literature, or recommendations, or rules of thumb etc, relating to this I would be interested to see it.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

interesting question and I think a quite common problem with landuse data in regression analyses such as occupancy models.

I don't know anything formal about how to treat this but your approach looks interesting to me. In a sense, you treat your landcover predictor as something intermediate between a categorical and a continuous explanatory variable. Sounds good to me.

The other (obvious) thing that comes to my mind when you worry that the preponderance of zeroes affects your ability to detect effects of a predictor in the nonzero range is to simply repeat the analysis with the zeros dropped. But this way you may end up with very few cases (because the zeroes will typically be in different cases for different predictors). Plus, the zeroes aren't missing values, they are zeroes, so throwing them out isn't really the right thing to do either (except for an informal exploratory analysis; that's what I suggest).

So, in summary, I don't know a definite answer either ....

Best regards  --- Marc

Hi all,

I am simulating data sets from a three-level hierarchical model as that described in Hostetler & Chandler(2015) <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/14-1487.1/full> with the pcountOpen argument dynamics="trend".

I have M sites that are visited over T primary periods. In words these are the levels (details in Hostetler & Chandler 2015):

1)  the initial number of individuals available to detection at each site varies according to a Poisson with a certain parameter (lambda).

2) the  number of individuals available to detection after the first primary period at each site depends on a Poisson whose parameter is the product of the number of individuals at the previous primary period times the growth rate (gamma).

3) the number of individuals detected at each site and primary period depends on a Binomial distribution that picks up a certain number of individuals from those available according to a certain parameter (detectability).

I have built the data sets in such a way that all the parameters, lambda, gamma, and detectability, depend linearly each one on a different predictor (distributed uniformly around zero).  Lambda and detectability depends on predictors varying across sites (no over time) and gamma depends on a predictor varying over time (no across sites).

Below some details on the parameter values I have used to simulate the data set. I don't give details on the predictors since I am interested here just on the average of each parameter (i.e. the intercept):

> mean.lambda<- 20 # when back-transformed this will be a Poisson around this value (no. of individuals)

> alpha1<- log(mean.lambda) # on the log scale this is the value of the intercept for lambda

> beta1<- 2 # this is the slope for lambda (on the log scale)

> mean.gamma<- 1 # this is the average growth rate (1= stable population)

> alpha2<- log(mean.gamma)# on the log scale this is the value of the intercept for gamma

> beta2<- 1 # this is the slope for gamma (on the log scale)

> mean.detectability<- 0.05 # this is the average detection probability

> alpha3<- qlogis(mean.detectability) # on the logit scale this is the value of the intercept for the detection probability

> beta3<- 3 # this is the slope for the detection probability (on the logit scale)

Then I run a pcountOpen model with the 'true' predictors and want to assess the accuracy of estimates by using the RSS (Residual Sum of Squares) on the back-transformed average estimate of each parameter (lambda, gamma, and detectability): I vary the K values like this:

m200<- pcountOpen(~A1, ~A2, ~1, ~KR, data= data$umf, dynamics= "trend", K= 200)

m300<- pcountOpen(~A1, ~A2, ~1, ~KR, data= data$umf, dynamics= "trend", K= 300)

I have been reading the Dennis et al. interesting question and I think a quite common problem with landuse data in regression analyses such as occupancy models.

I don't know anything formal about how to treat this but your approach looks interesting to me. In a sense, you treat your landcover predictor as something intermediate between a categorical and a continuous explanatory variable. Sounds good to me.

The other (obvious) thing that comes to my mind when you worry that the preponderance of zeroes affects your ability to detect effects of a predictor in the nonzero range is to simply repeat the analysis with the zeros dropped. But this way you may end up with very few cases (because the zeroes will typically be in different cases for different predictors). Morning all,

I have been fitting some occupancy (and other) models recently using covariates that are highly skewed / zero-inflated. This question is not really realted to unmarked the package, but I feel like the answer, which I am sure some of you will have, will be inforamtive for unamrked analyses (but apologies if i am wrong!).

I am trying to find some guidance on how to treat highly skewed / zero-inflated PREDICTORS in a model, say a landcover type where ~80 % of the data are 0’s and 20% >0. In my head it seems clear to me that the zeros add an enormous amount of noise that detract from estimating a relationship of interest that exists in the non-zero parameter space. My current thinking about this issue would be to model the zeros explicitly:

y_{i} = b_{0} + b_{1} * I(cov=0) + b_{2} * cov + e_{i}

i.e., an intercept for the zeros and a coefficient for the relationship in the non-zero space. I did a small simulation study to see if a simple regression model can recover parameters from data generated under this model and it all checks out, but is it the recommended thing to do? Imagine also if all 5 or 20 or whatever covariates were like this?

Okay, so in short, I know that there are typically no assumptions about the distribution of the predictors in regression type analyses, so I am wondering, although the predictor has no assumed distribution, does a large amount of zero inflation influence the ability to detect an effect of the non-zero stuff.

If anyone knows of some literature, or recommendations, or rules of thumb etc, relating to this I would be interested to see it.

Chris

Chris, this is definitely an interesting, common, and tricky problem.  From a linear model standpoint, a severe skew in the distribution of your covariate means that certain bins of values (if you were to discretize the measure) have large sample sizes while others have small.  So the problem is that your regression coefficients are potentially going to be poorly estimated, since only a few samples contribute to the slope estimates with those samples having high leverage.

Some kind of transformation would make sense here, I think, and with so many zeros something like a square root might work.  Then your hypothesis is about the multiplicative effect of the covariate, which may or may not make sense.  But I like your covariate set up too, similar to a hurdle model.

Hi Eric,

1).  If the purpose is to compare these two methods, then I think you don't want to use option 1, because psi/z will be method specific and potentially very different, thus defeating the purpose of comparison.

2).  Regarding option #2: do you mean sampling covariate? If different sampling methods were used at each site (such that you trapped one week, and snorkeled around another week) I think treating method as a visit covariate would be very reasonable.  If a site was sampled using trapping or visual id exclusively, then the comparison seems a little more tenuous to me, but I think using method as a site covariate for p might be your best option.

3).  If these different sampling methods were simultaneously occurring in slightly different patch subunits, multi-method or multi-scale models (Nichols et al. 2008, journal of applied ecology) might be a good option.  If the methods were sampling exactly the same place at the same time (i.e., independence of observations seems unlikely), then the Nichols et al. model might not appropriately describe the variance, but I think this would still be your best bet.

Just my 0.02.  I would be curious to hear anybody else's take on using method as a site-covariate for p.

Cheers,

John

messages.subject_clean: Designing an occupancy study with "nebulous seasons"
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

My student and I are designing a study of dynamic occupancy for a woodpecker species.  We would like to assess prob of occupancy, colonization and extinction of certain habitat types between seasons (and possibly between years) by sampling each survey point twice in the breeding season and twice in the non-breeding season (and then replicating this in a second year).  I am used to working with species that have relatively defined breeding and non-breeding seasons, and from our reading, it seems that this WP species is territorial in both seasons, but can also be somewhat nomadic and start migrating at any time in the spring (though most wait until late April).

My question is how best to design the study with regard to the timing of surveys.  Can we just sample consistently across seasons, once all 150 points are sampled, start again for round 2, from Feb though July.  OR, Should we not survey during the times generally thought to be peak migration?  Each survey is broken down into 4 periods so we can estimate detection prob from one survey and only assume closure within a survey (not between), so I suspect this is ok, but wanted some feedback if possible.

Thanks so much in advance for your thoughts.

Lesley Bulluck

# Just two parameters

n0<-exp(parms[3])

# add a row of zeros onto the matrix
 y2d<- rbind(y2d, rep(0,K))
# a vector to hold the result

Hi Chris and others

I find this to be a timely post because today I encountered this issue with a student's question asked in a workshop I'm co-instructing and I didn't have a clear answer.  Thus far, the student's approach was to standardize the covariate (i.e., % cover type) for an occupancy analysis in which the raw covariate values contained mostly 0% values. I'm not sure whether or not this is an appropriate approach, but am interested in the consequences in taking such an approach.  Perhaps simulating under this scenario could shed some light on it's utility. I will share any insights that come out of working on this with the student, but I would like to hear opinions from others on standardization of "zero-inflated" covariates.

Chris, perhaps cross-posting this question to the hmecology forum would prompt responses from a larger audience.

Jared

Here is something I did recently to do some preliminary feeling out of the issue (make of it what you will – it seems obvious that if I simulate from the ‘hurdle model’ it does better):

#------- start of previous email correspondence code below figure:

I wanted to see whether a regression analysis could recover the two ‘means’ and a single slope pertaining to the z=1 class of the discretization of the continuous variable.

If you are interested, you can execute the following code and see that the model can recover the parameters extremely well.

This makes me think that adding both versions (binary and continuous) of a covariate seems to be okay.

What is clear here is that IF the data are generated under the ‘hurdle’ process, the excess 0’s screw things up when you treat the covariates as continuous – I didn’t scale the covariate, but I can’t see it making the difference??

***disclaimer*** This is a quick and dirty simulation – feel free to tell I am wrong.

set.seed(1)

sims <- 1000

out <- array(NA,c(sims,3,3))

coefs <- c("(Intercept)","bin","cont")

ac <- adjustcolor(c(2,3,4),alpha.f=0.3)

for(i in 1:sims){

bin <- rep(c(0,1),each=100) #binary data

cont <- runif(200,2,20) * bin #”zero-inflated” covariate

mu <- 20 + bin * 50 + 3 * cont

y <- rnorm(length(mu),mu,10)

fm1 <- lm(y ~ bin + cont)

fm2 <- lm(y ~ cont)

fm3 <- lm(y ~ bin)

out[i,,1] <- coef(fm1)[coefs]

out[i,,2] <- coef(fm2)[coefs]

out[i,,3] <- coef(fm3)[coefs]

par(mfrow=c(1,3))

Mathias

hi Nicole,
 if we ever get distsampOpen working, it will only handle distance sampling data with a population dynamics model, not mixed DS and multinomial data (note: this is something that would be good to have at some point but we don't have the time to do it; if anyone in the community has an interest in writing such extensions then this is something we'd be interested in).

andy

messages.body_plain:
I would add that designing your survey to maximize detection of your species is always a good thing.  People conduct point counts within 5 hours of sunrise because that's when songbirds vocalize the most during the breeding season.  You could sample beyond the morning, and model time since sunrise as a detection covariate, but then there will be more uncertainty about the state process for sites with late surveys.  If those are the data you have, that's one thing, but if you have control over the design then there are better choices to be made.

Regarding your design, Lesley, the date of surveys could be modeled to account for migration, but it would certainly be better to avoid this additional uncertainty if you had the choice.  Another good resource for this topic is Nichols et al. 2009 (below) where they discuss the components of the observation process for birds, which are more complex than some folks appreciate.  Many would agree that availability is the trickiest problem for point counts and you need to understand how your survey design addresses it (e.g., plot size, temporal replication, etc.).

Nichols, J. D., L. Thomas, and P. B. Conn.  2009.  Inferences about landbird abundance from count data: Recent advances and future directions.  Pages 201-235 in D. L. Thomson, E. G. Cooch, and M. J. Conroy, editors.  Modeling Demographic Processes in Marked Populations.  Springer, New York.

> we have now mentioned our new book a couple of times on this list, so let's make it official and formal once and for all.
>
> Our new book Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology (Academic Press, 2016), or AHM for short, provides an up-to-date synthesis on the hierarchical modeling of abundance, occurrence and community metrics such as species richness in what we call "meta-population designs". By the latter, we mean the very common case where you have measured these things at multiple sites. That is, the typical data collection protocol for occupancy and N-mixture models etc. Not surprisingly, one big feature of almost all the models in our book is an explicit model component for measurement error (that is, typically for false-negative errors).

Dear unmarked-list'ers,

the latest version of AICcmodavg (2.0-4) is now on CRAN. Changes relevant to unmarked users include:

1) modavgPred (for model-averaged predictions) now computes confidence intervals (back-transformed from the link scale, when modavgPred(, type = "response"). These values are now stored in a matrix called "matrix.output".

2) a new function to compute the covariance diagnostic ("sparseness indicator") based on Dennis et al. (2015: Biometrics 71:237-246.) for the single season N-mixture model.

3) three new functions to get quick summary statistics/plots and diagnose potential data issues:  detHist (for binary detection data), countHist (for count data), countDist (for distance sampling data). For example, you can use detHist to determine the number of sites with "observed colonization" or "observed extinction" events for each season from the detection history data. These functions work with the unmarkedFrame data classes as well as unmarkedFit objects. For LaTeX users, I also added xtable methods for tables output by these functions.

Sincerely,

Marc M.

Hi Marc,

This is a great package!

I am having an issue (possible bug?) with the modavgPred() function. The output table in the console looks fine however when attempting to grab (or plot) from the lower.CL column, a chr of length 1 is returned "lower.CL". This is also seen when calling the str() function on the output. Grabbing the upper.CL column works fine however not for lower.CL.

Here is some code showing the problem with the mallard dataset.

data(mallard)
mallardUMF <- unmarkedFramePCount(mallard.y, siteCovs = mallard.site,
                                  obsCovs = mallard.obs)
##set up models so that each variable on abundance appears twice
fm.mall.one <- pcount(~ ivel + date ~ length + forest, mallardUMF,
                      K = 30)
fm.mall.two <- pcount(~ ivel + date ~ elev + forest, mallardUMF,
                      K = 30)
fm.mall.three <- pcount(~ ivel + date ~ length + elev, mallardUMF,
                        K = 30)
fm.mall.four <- pcount(~ ivel + date ~ 1, mallardUMF, K = 30)

##model list
Cands <- list(fm.mall.one, fm.mall.two, fm.mall.three, fm.mall.four)
Modnames <- c("length + forest", "elev + forest", "length + elev",
              "null")
##compute model-averaged predictions of abundance for values of elev
output <- modavgPred(cand.set = Cands, modnames = Modnames, newdata =
             data.frame(elev = seq(from = -1.4, to = 2.4, by = 0.1),
                        length = 0, forest = 0), parm.type = "lambda",
           type = "response")

plot(output$mod.avg.pred, seq(from = -1.4, to = 2.4, by = 0.1), type = "l")
lines(output$upper.CL, seq(from = -1.4, to = 2.4, by = 0.1), type = "l", col = "red", lty = 2)
plot(output$lower.CL, seq(from = -1.4, to = 2.4, by = 0.1), type = "l")

output$lower.CL[1]
output$lower.CL[2]

str(output)

Thanks!

Eric

Ken
